Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,
closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 4:00 pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be
summarized by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City
Council and will also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be
recorded for public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

Comments From The Audience - Non-Agenda Items
During this time, members of the public may address the City Council regarding any items not
listed on the agenda and within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council and not on
this agenda. Comments from the audience will be limited to three (3) minutes per speaker;
unless authorized by the Mayor, the time limit may not be extended by utilizing another
member's time. There will be no debate or action on items not listed on the agenda unless
authorized by law. The collective initial period of time for comments from the audience shall
be limited to 45 minutes. Any speaker that did not get a chance to speak during this segment

  3
 due to the 45-minute limitations will be able to speak at the end of the meeting prior to
adjournment.

Note: The City Council desires to provide all members of the public with the opportunity to
address the Council. Nevertheless, obscene language, comments intended to
disrupt/interfere, other actions which disrupt the progress of the meeting or slanderous
comments will not be tolerated and may result in ejection and/or may constitute a violation of
South Gate Municipal Code Section1.04.110.

Reports And Comments From City Officials
During this time, members of the City Council will report on matters pertaining to their service
on various intergovernmental boards and commissions as a representative of the City
pursuant to Assembly Bill 1234. City Council Members will also have an opportunity to
comment on matters not on the agenda.

Consent Calendar Items
Agenda Items 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 are Consent Calendar Items. All items including Ordinances,
Resolutions and Contracts, may be approved by adoption of the Consent Calendar,
individually and collectively by one (1) motion. There will be no separate discussion of these
items unless Members of the City Council, the public, or staff request that specific items be
removed from the Consent Calendar for separate discussion and action. Members of the
public are permitted to speak on any item listed but their time period is limited to three (3)
minutes in total.

Any motion to introduce or adopt an Ordinance on the Consent Calendar shall be: (1) a
motion to waive the reading of the Ordinance and introduce the Ordinance or (2) a motion to
waive the reading of the Ordinance and adopt the Ordinance, as appropriate.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

  7
 PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such
times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

  NOTICINGREQUIREMENTS:  TheNoticeofPublicHearingfortheCity's2025UWMPandWSCP
  was published inthe LosAngeles  Wave newspaper on May 14, 2026, and May 21, 2026, and was posted

  ANALYSIS:  State law requires urban water suppliers that provide more than 3,000 acre-feet of water
  annually or maintain more than 3,000 service connections to prepare and update an {JWMP every five
  years. The City is required to comply with these requirements because it serves approximately 14,400
  water service connections and delivers approximately 8,000 acre-feet of water annually. The 'UWMP

  9
 serves as the City's  long-range  water  supply  plaru"iing  document  and demonstrates  that sufficient  water
supplies  are  available  to meet current  and future  community  needs.
State law also requires  the City to prepare  and adopt a Water  Shortage  Contingency  Plan (WSCP),  which
outlines  how water  supplies  would  be managed  during  droughts  and other water  shortage  emergencies.

The City's  current  UWMP  WSCP  was adopted  in 2021.  The updated  2025 UWMP  and WSCP  must be
adopted  and submitted  to the California  Department  of Water  Resources  by July  1, 2026.  Failure  to
comply  with  these requirements  could  affect  the City's  eligibility  for certain  State and Federal  water-
related  grants,  loans,  and drought  assistance  programs.

The  City  has  completed  both  documents  and  is  seeking  City  Council  adoption  to  satisfy  State
requirements.  The 2025 UWMP  concludes  that the City  has sufficient  water  supplies  and groundwater
pumping  allocations  to meet projected  water  demands  throughout  the 25-year  planning  horizon,  while
the WSCP  provides  a framework  for responding  to future  droughts  and water  shortage  emergencies.

BACKGROUND:  The 2025 UWMP  is a long-term  resource  planning  tool that assesses existing  and
future  potable  water  resources  and water  demands.  It identifies  measures  for managing  water  demand,
including  conservation  programs,  implementation  strategies,  public  outreach,  education  efforts,  and
water  savings  analyses.

The 2025 UWMP  requires  urban  water  suppliers  to report  projected  water  use in five-year  increments
over a 25-year  planning  horizon  in accordance  with  Water  Code Section  10635(a).  The Plan evaluates
past,  present,  and  projected  conditions  regarding  population,  demographics,  climate  trends,  water
production,  water  consumption,  and conservation  measures.

The 2025 UWMP  includes  a Water  Shortage  Contingency  Plan (WSCP),  which  outlines  the actions  the
City may implement  during  water  shortage  emergencies  and drought  conditions.  The WSCP  establishes
response  actions  and  corresponding  conservation  measures  for  six  standard  water  shortage  levels
pursuant  to State Water  Code requirements.

Key findings  of the 2025 UWMP  include  the following:

  *  The City's  water  system  continues  to be supported  primarily  by groundwater  from  the Central
  Basin,  which  remains  capable  of meeting  projected  potable  water  demands  over  the planning
  horizon.  The  City  maintains  emergency  interconnections  with  neighboring  agencies  and
  Metropolitan  Water  District  (MWD)  connections  to supplement  supply  if necessary.

  @  The City  maintains  sufficient  water  rights  and pumping  allocations  to meet projected  customer
  demands.  The annual  Allowed  Pumping  Allocation  (APA)  continues  to exceed  projected  annual
  demand.

  *  The  City  has continued  implementing  water  conservation  requirements  consistent  with  State
  mandates,  including  Senate Bill  x7-7  and newer  water  use efficiency  regulations  established  by
  the State.

  *  The City's  water  conservation  efforts  include  permanent  water  waste prohibitions,  full metering,
  conservation-based  pricing  structures,  public  outreach,  distribution  system  loss monitoring,  and
  ongoing  meter  replacement  and infrastruchire  improvement  programs.

  1  10
   *  The  City  continues  to participate  in regional  conservation  partnerships  and rebate  programs
  offered  through  the Central  Basin  Municipal  Water  District  (CBMWD)  and the Metropolitan
  Water  District  of Southern  California  (MWD),  including  programs  supporting  turf replacement,
  high-efficiency  fixtures,  and commercial  water  use improvements.

  *  The WSCP  establishes  response  actions  for progressive  shortage  levels  and provides  flexibility
  for the City Council  to adopt additional  conservatiorx  regulations  in response  to future  State Water
  Resources  Control  Board  emergency  regulations  or regional  drought  conditions.

  The UWMP  demonstrates  that the City  is projected  to maintain  adequate  water  supplies  to meet
  customer  demands  under  normal  operating  conditions  throughout  the 25-year  planning  period.

 BACKGROUND:

Water  Rates  and Revenue
The City  operates  its water  system  as an enterprise  fund.  An enterprise  fund  is a self-supporting
account  funded  by the rates customers  pay, kept  separate  from  the City's  General  Fund.  Water
rates are set to cover the cost of operating  and maintaining  the system,  paying  debt service  on past
infrastructure  borrowing,  funding  capital  projects,  and maintaining  reserves.

Annual  water  rate revenue  is approximately  equal  to annual  operating  costs plus  debt  service,
totaling  about  $22 million  per year. Because  revenue  and costs are closely  matched,  current  rates
add little  or no new money  to reserves  in a typical  year.

The City's  most recent  water  rate study was completed  in June 2011,  and the last rate adjustment
took effect  in Fiscal  Year 2015-16.

Outstanding  Water  Bonds  and Rate  Covenant
The Water  Fund  has two  outstanding  revenue  bond  series:  the 2019  Series  A Water  Revenue
Refunding  Bonds  (tax-exempt)  and  the  2019  Series  A-T  Water  Revenue  Refunding  Bonds
(taxable).  These  bonds,  with  combined  outstanding  principal  of approximately  $21.1  million,
refunded  the City's  2012  Water  Revenue  Bonds  and are secured  by net water  system  revenues.
Combined  annual  debt  service  is approximately  $2.5  million  per year  and is essentially  level
through  final  maturity  in Fiscal  Year 2035-36.

The bonds  include  a rate covenant  requiring  that net water  system  revenues  equal  at least 1.15
times  annual  debt service,  or approximately  $2.9 million  per year. Because  the proposed  program
does not change  water  rates, the underlying  rate structure  continues  to produce  the same revenue
per unit  of water  delivered.  The Water  Fund  also earns investment  income  on its accumulated
balance,  and projected  net revenues  exceed  the  l.l5x  threshold  under  each discount  scenario
presented  in this report.

Water  Fund  Balance  and Reserves
The water  fund holds  an accumulated  balance  of approximately  $57 million.  This balance  built  up
over  time  and is one-time  monies  programmed  for  infrastructure  improvements;  it is not  an
ongoing  annual  surplus.  As  shown  below,  about  $10  million  is maintained  as operating  and
emergency  reserves  under  the City's  adopted  Budget  & Financial  Policies,  leaving  about  $47
million  of one-time  a  available  for  a  jects.

The  City's  Capital  Improvement  Program  (CIP)  is the City's  multi-year  plan  and budget  for
building,  replacing,  and upgrading  infrastruchire.  The CIP identifies  a large  and growing  list of
water  system  needs. Major  categories  include:

  standards.  The City has a $13 million  treatment  system in design  (Phase I) and an additional
  $9 million  system  planned  (Phase II).
  Water  main  and pipeline  replacements,  including  a $6 million  Phase III pipeline  project  in

  Meter  modernization  (AMR/AMI)  [Automated  Meter  Reading  / Advanced  Metering

ANALYSIS:

Water  Fund  Financial  Context
Three  facts frame  the analysis.  First,  water  rate revenue  (about  $22 million  per year)  is roughly

How  the Conditional,  One-Time  Discount  Would  Work
The concept  is a one-time  discount  applied  to water bills  for City  water  customers  over a defined
period  (for example,  about one year),  taking  effect  only in the event the UUT  measure  is approved
by voters.  The City  Council  could  adopt  a resolution  in advance  that describes  the discount  and
expressly  conditions  it on the measure's  passing.

It is important  to accurately  describe  the discount.  Water  rates themselves  would  not  change.
Instead,  the City  would  apply  temporary  credits  to bills,  reducing  the revenue  the City  actually
collects  during  the program  period.  Tis  is best understood  as revenue  not billed,  not as the City
writing  checks  from  a pile of surplus  cash.

Because  less revenue  is billed  and subsequently  collected,  less money  flows  into the water  fund
that year. The effect  is a deferral  of capital  funding:  with  less cash available,  some planned  capital
work  must be delayed,  phased  differently,  or resized.  Given  that Phase I is funded  and protected,
the practical  effect  of a discount  falls  on the timing  of Phase II projects.

JThy a multi-year  discount  is not recommended
A one-time  discount  uses one-time  capacity.  Repeating  the discount  over  multiple  years  would
compound  the impact  on the water  fund  and the CIP,  delay  more  projects,  and threaten  system
reliability  and regulatory  compliance.  Delaying  capital  projects  is further  not advisable  because
project  costs generally  increase  over time  due to inflation,  resulting  in higher  future  expenditures
for the same improvements.  It would  also likely  require  larger  future  rate increases  once  the
program  ended.  For these reasons,  staff would  not recommend  a multi-year  structure.

Long-Term  Funding Outlook and Future Rate Adiustment
Apart from  the discount,  the water  fund  faces  a structural  funding  gap. Annual  rate revenue  of
about $22 million  roughly  matches  operating  and debt service  costs, so current  rates do not rebuild
reserves.  The $47 million  one-time  capacity  is finite  and is being  drawn  down  by the funded  and
planned  capital  program,  and the $80 million  of Phase III  needs  is entirely  unfunded.  For these
reasons,  the City  will  likely  need a water  rate adjustment  within  approximately  the next two  to
three years  to keep the 'fund healthy  and stable.

This need exists  independently  of the proposed  discount  and of the UUT  measure;  it is driven  by
capital  needs and by rates that do not replenish  reserves.  If a discount  is adopted,  it would  reduce
one year of collected  revenue  and could  affect  the timing  of a future  rate adjustment,  but it is not
the cause of the underlying  need.

The amount  and timing  of any rate adjustment  would  be determined  by an updated  cost-of-service
rate study  and set through  the Proposition  218 majority-protest  process,  which  requires  mailed
notice  to affected  parcels,  apublic  hearing,  and separate Council  action.  No rate change  is proposed
or decided  by this report.  Staff  intend  to bring  an updated  rate study  forward  in advance  of any
proposed  adjustment  so the Council  and the public  can review  the basis before  any decision.

  ANALYSIS:  The City is currently facing a General Fund budget deficit exceeding $9.4 Million,
  As part of the Fiscal Year 2026/27 budget development process, all departments were directed to
  identify expenditure reductions to help address the City's fiscal challenges. On June 9, 2026, the

  1

  37
 City Council approved the Fiscal Year 2026/27 0perating  Budget, which incorporated  a variety of
cost-saving measures recommended by departments.

Public Works evaluated multiple budget reduction opportunities. However, because many Public
Works programs are supported by enterprise funds, special revenue funds, grants, and other
restricted funding sources, opportunities to reduce General Fund-supported expenditures were
limited. As a result, staff evaluated operational changes within existing programs that could
generate meaningful savings while maintaining service levels.

Under Contract No. 2022-83-CC, United Pacific Services, Inc. (UPS) provides comprehensive
citywide tree maintenance services. The agreement established a four-year grid trimming cycle
and includes a provision allowing the contract to be extended annually, for up to four one-year
terms, subject to City Council approval. As part of the budget reduction evaluation, staff assessed
the operational and financial impacts of extending the tree trimming cycle from four years to five
years. Based on maintenance needs, service demands, and available resources, staff determined
that a five-year cycle is operationally feasible and would continue to provide an acceptable level
of service wile reducing annual contract costs by approximately $127,348.

This cost-saving measure was incorporated into the Fiscal Year 2026/27 0perating  Budget
approved by the City Coiu'icil. Amendment No. 3 to Contract No. 2022-83-CC implements that
budget reduction by modifying the tree trimming cycle from four years to five years and exercising
the next available one-year contract extension through June 30, 2027. The amendment will allow
the City to continue providing essential urban forest maintenance services while aligning program
expenditures with current fiscal conditions.

Staff  also  evaluated rebidding the contract to determine whether sufficient savings could be
achieved  to  maintain the existing four-year trimming  cycle. However, the City is currently
benefiting  from pricing  established in 2022/23, and annual adjustments have historically  been
limited  to CPI-based increases that have been mutually acceptable to boththe City and UPS. Given
current market conditions and increased labor, equipment, fuel, and insurance costs, staff expects
that a new solicitation  would result in higher pricing. As a result, rebidding the contract is not
expected  to generate savings and would likely increase the cost of maintaining the City's tree
maintenance  program.

While  tree trimming  cycles vary among municipalities  based on urban forest conditions, service
expectations,  and available funding, five-year trimming cycles are not uncommon within the urban
forestry  industry. In addition, the City recently implemented a comprehensive hazard mitigation
effort through  Amendment No. 1 to Contract No. 2022-83-CC, which funded the removal of dead,
diseased,  distressed, and structurally compromised trees, as well as corrective maintenance on
higher-risk  trees identified through a citywide urban forest assessment. As a result of these
proactive  measures,  combined with ongoing tree maintenance activities and continued funding for
emergency  response,  hazardous tree trimming, and resident service requests, staff believes the
City's urban forest can be effectively maintained under a five-yeartrimming  cycle while continuing
to provide an acceptable level of service and public safety while achieving necessary budgetary
savings.

BACKGROUND:  The City owns and maintains an urban forest consisting of more than 17,500
  located throughout public streets, parks, medians, and City facilities. These trees requtre

 ongoing  maintenance  to support  public  safety,  tree health,  visibility,  and protection  of public

The Public  Works  Department  oversees  the City's  urban  forestry  program  through  a contracted
tree maintenance  provider.  On September  27, 2022, the City  Council  approved  ContractNo.  2022-
83-CC  with  United  Pacific  Services,  Inc.  (UPS)  in  an amount  not  to  exceed  $3,789,545,
establishing  a four-year  contract  term and a four-year  grid trirnrning  cycle.  Under  the agreement,
UPS provides  comprehensive  citywide  tree maintenance  services,  including  grid  trimming,  tree
removals,  emergency  response,  and ongoing  care of the City's  urban forest,  which  consists  of more
than 17,500  trees.

On September  26, 2023,  the City  Council  approved  Amendment  No. 1 to Contract  No. 2022-83-
CC, increasing  the contract  amount  by $861,425  to fiind priority  tree maintenance  services,  annual
off-cycle  special  trims,  and well  site tree trimming  at the Hawkins  Water  Production  Facility.  The
amendment  was  necessary  to  implement  recommendations  from  a citywide  urban  forest
assessment  that  identified  a significant  backlog  of dead,  diseased,  distressed,  and structurally
compromised  trees posing  potential  risks  to public  safety.  The assessment  categorized  trees into
Priority  1, 2, and  3 risk  levels  based  on the  urgency  of  corrective  action  needed.  Because
addressing  these  hazardous  conditions  required  resources  beyond  the  scope  of  the  original
agreement,  Amendment  No.  1 provided  supplemental  funding  to accelerate  the  removal  and
maintenance  of high-risk  trees throughout  the City.

In April  2025,  Amendment  No.  2 to Contract  No.  2022-83-CC  was executed,  reallocating  the
amount  balances  within  the original  submitted  bid  schedule  for  Year  3 of the  contract  (FY
2024/25).  Specifically,  adjustments  were  made  to individual  bid  items  including  reductions  to
annual  grid trimming,  off-cycle  special  request  trimming,  and tree installation  services,  offset  by
increases  to tree and stump  removal  and crew rental  services.  The total  contract  amount  for Year
3 remained  unchanged  at $1,145,098,  and no changes  were made to the scope of work.

Staff worked  with  the contractor  to assess transitioning  from  a four-year  to five-year  tree trirnrning
cycle.  Tree trimming  cycles  are periodically  reviewed  to balance  service  levels,  operational  needs,
risk management,  and available  funding.  Under  the current  four-year  cycle,  approximately  14,000
parkway  trees are trimmed  unevenly  by geographic  zones, with  approximately  2,792 trees trimmed
in Year  1, 3,601  trees in Year  2, 5,059  trees in Year  3, and 3,232  trees in Year  4, resulting  in
fluctuating  annual  workloads  and costs, with  the current  trimming  schedule  producing  significant
annual  workload  variations  between  maintenance  zones.

The proposed  five-year  cycle  would  distribute  trirnrning  activities  more  evenly,  creating  a more
balanced  and sustainable  maintenance  program  while  reducing  annual  costs  by approximately
$127,348.  The  contract  will  continue  to include  fiinding  for  special  tree trimming  services  to
address  hazardous  conditions,  priority  locations,  emergency  response  work,  and resident  service
requests  outside  of the regular  trimming  cycle.

Palm  tree maintenance,  which  is typically  performed  on a more  frequent  cycle  due to species-
specific  requirements,  will  continue  under  its  current  maintenance  schedule  and  will  not  be
impacted  by the proposed  transition  to a five-year  cycle.  Tree maintenance  services  within  City
parks  will  also continue  to be supported  through  contributions  from  the Parks  and Recreation
Department.

 ANALYSIS:  KOA  Corporation  is currently  under  contract  to prepare  the design  and constniction
documents  for  the  Intersection  Improvements  Project.  While  the  majority  of  the  proposed
improvements  are located  within  public  street rights-of-way,  portions  of the project  impact  property
and facilities  owned  by the Los  Angeles  Department  of Water  and Power  (LADWP),  including
improvements  at intersections  along  Southern  Avenue  that are under  shared jurisdiction.

As part of its review  process,  LADWP  has required  additional  engineering  documentation  that was
not included  in the original  scope  of services.  Specifically,  LADWP  requires  a detailed  survey  of
existing  overhead  electrical  conductors  and the identification  of all proposed  improvements  with
corresponding  elevations  and coordinated  data. To satisfy  these requirements  and obtain  LADWP
approval  of the project  plans  and permits,  KOA  Corporation  must  perform  additional  surveying
work  and update  the project  plans,  specifications,  and supporting  design  documents.

Amendment  No.  1 provides  the  additional  design  engineering  services  necessary  to  address
LADWP  requirements  for the three  affected  intersections  along  Southern  Avenue.  The cost of the
additional  services  is $43,628,  as reflected  in proposed  Amendment  No. 1.

BACKGROUND:  The Intersection  Improvements  Project  is included  in the Fiscal  Year  2025/26
Capital  Improvement  Program  and is intended  to improve  pedestrian  safety  and  accessibility  at
seven intersections  located  along  Southern  Avenue  and California  Avenue.  Planned  improvements
include  a traffic  signal  modification  to provide  protected  left-turn  phasing  at the intersection  of
California  Avenue  and  Santa  Ana  Street.  Improvements  at the  remaining  project  intersections
include  pedestrian-activated  flashing  beacons,  high-visibility  crosswalks,  updated  signage  and
pavement  markings,  curb  ramp  upgrades,  and other  pedestrian  safety  enhancements  designed  to
improve  visibility  and reduce  conflicts  between  motorists  and pedestrians  along  Southern  Avenue
and California  Avenue.

Three  of the project  intersections  located  along  Southern  Avenue  include  improvements  that  are
partially  situated  within  property  and right-of-way  owned  by the Los Angeles  Department  of Water
and Power  (LADWP).  As  a result,  the proposed  improvements  are subject  to LADWP  review,
approval,  and permitting  requirements  prior  to construction.

On May  9, 2023,  the City  Council  approved  Contract  No.  2023-60-CC  with  KOA  Corporation  in
the  amount  of  $194,647  to  provide  engineering  design  services  and  prepare  the  plans,
specifications,  and estimates  necessary  for project  construction.  Design  is currently  underway  and is
nearing  completion.

During  LADWP's  review  of the project,  additional  design  requirements  were  identified  for  the
improvements  located  within  LADWP  property.  Specifically,  LADWP  requires  supplemental
surveying  and  engineering  documentation,  including  the  identification  of  existing  overhead
electrical  facilities  and  the  preparation  of  design  information  with  associated  elevations  and
coordinating  data. These requirements  were not included  in the original  scope of services.

To satisfy  LADWP's  permitting  requirements  and obtain  approval  of the project  plans,  additional
engineering  design  services  are necessary.  Amendment  No.  1 to Contract  No.  2023-60-CC  in the
amount  of  $43,628  will  fund  the  additional  surveying,  design,  and  plan  preparation  services
required  to update  the project  plans and specifications  and advance  the project  toward  construction.

SCOPE OF WORK
TASK  101  - ADDITIONAL  PROJECT  MANAGEMENT

The scope and duration  of project  services  have extended  beyond  the original  two-year  schedule  and we are now
approaching  year four of the project.  While  our team  has continued  to provide  consistent  project  management  support  to
maintain  quality,  schedule  and stakeholder  communication,  the additional  effort  required  to manage  the extended
timeline  has exceeded  the original  budget  allocation.

The initial  project  management  budget  was originally  based on a two-year  schedule,  which  projected  construction  and as-
built  plans to be completed  by December  2024. However,  as of December  2025, the project  is currently  at the 90% design
phase, with  construction  completion  now anticipated  for December  2026. Within  this extended  schedule,  we have
accounted  for 44 hours of additional  project  management  and meeting  time  between  January  2025 to December  2025.
The additional  budget  will allow  KOA to attend  additional  progress  meetings,  sustain  the same level of technical  support,
documentation,  and inter-agency  coordination  necessary  to deliver  the project  successfully  and in alignment  with client
expectations.  A portion  of the additional  project  management  budget  (42 hours)  will be applied  to the additional  project
management  hours spent  between  January  2026 to December  2026.

TASK  102  - LADWP  COORDINATION  AND  SUPPORT

AS-NEEDED  COORDINATION  & SUPPORT  ALLOWANCE

LADWP coordination  was not included  in the original  project  scope or budget.  As the project  has progressed,  the City has
identified  the need for additional  engagement  with  LADWP  to address  design  considerations,  right-of-way  impacts  and
additional  studies  to satisfy  agency  needs. While  the City will continue  to lead all primary  LADWP coordination  efforts,  the
City has requested  KOA to participate  in a supporting  role to ensure  the project  remains  technically  sounds  and compliant
with  LADWP  requirements.

This support  includes  reviewing  LADWP  plan comments,  attending  coordination  meetings  as requested  by the City, and
providing  technical  input  or revisions  as needed  to maintain  design  accuracy.  These activities  were not anticipated  in the
initial  scope,  but are necessary  to ensure  the project  components  remain  coordinated  and fully  integrated  with  LADWP
standards.

TASK 1-  PROJECT  MANAGEMENT  / ADMINISTRATION  / MEETINGS
Giuseppe  Canzonieri,  PE, will be the Project  Manager.  He is a senior  engineer  with 16 years of experience.
He has extensive  experience  in the field  of street  improvements,  pavement  rehabilitation,  geometric
design,  traffic  signal  design,  traffic  control  design,  pedestrian  facilities,  and handling  municipal  civil/traffic
engineering-related  services. He has also served as project  manager  and project  engineer  on many  civil/
traffic  engineering  design  projects  for several  cities  in Southern  California,  including  the City of South
Gate.

Our Project  Management  services  will include,  but not be limited  to:
  *  Attend  a virtual  kick-off  meeting  with  the City's  Project  Manager  and key staff to review  the
  project  in detail  and discuss  the City's  requirements.  We want  to make  sure everyone  involved  on
  our team  understands  the work  scope,  schedule,  budget,  and other  important  requirements  to
  make  the project  a success.
  Ensure the scope  of services  is completed  in a timely  and professional  manner.
  Attend  up to three  (3) meetings  with  City staff at the  30o*, 60o/o, and 90o/o design  stages.
  *  Attend  up to twelve  (12) virtual  monthly  progress  meetings.
  *  Maintain  communication  with  the City's  Project  Manager  throughout  the duration  of the project
  induding  PS&E package  status,  meeting  agendas  and minutes,  schedule  updates,  action  items,
  etc.
  *  Maintain  the project  schedule,  update  it regularly  to reflect  any significant  changes  in the project
  and keep the City informed  of these  changes.
  *  Coordinate  with  the City's  Project  Manager  to resolve  project  related  issues in a timely  manner.
  Potential  complex  issues will be brought  to the attention  of the City's  Project  Manager  as soon  as
  possible.
  *  Coordinate  and manage  KOA's  sub-consultants.
  Project  design  review.

It is our understanding  the City of South  Gate will be managing  and leading  the community  outreach
effort  with  in-house  staff.  KOA will provide  outreach  support  services  for City Staff in their  community
outreach  efforts.  KOA will:

  Attend  one (1 ) City Council  meeting,  provide  a PowerPoint  presentation,  and answer  questions  for
  the public,  committee,  or Council  members.
  Attend  up to two  (2) public  outreach  meetings  for business  owners  and residents  affected  by the
  project  within  the limits  of the project  and prepare  PowerPoint  presentation..  We are assuming
  that one (1) outreach  meeting  will be in-person  and one (1) will be virtual.

TASK  2 - AGENCY  AND  UTILITY  COORDINATION
KOA will obtain  a list from  the City of utility  companies  known  to own  and operate  facilities  in the City of
South  Gate. KOA will send an email  notice  with  our standard  utility  response  form,  and a map of the
project  site to all relevant  utility  companies.  We will request  information  from  them  including  record
drawings  of their  facilities,  prior  rights  information,  and any planned  upgrades  expected  in the near future.
Utility  responses  will be logged  and information  regarding  existing  facilities  will be shown  on our plans.  In
some  cases, the utility  owner  may require  a request  presented  on City letterhead.  We will coordinate  these
situations,  if needed,  with  the City's  Project  Manager.  KOA will provide  the City Project  Manager  with  a
utility  response  list and maps and/or  data received  when  all utility companies  have responded.  KOA will
compile  all as-builts  received  from  the utility  agencies  and develop  a utility  base map that  will be
referenced  into the project  plans.

Southern  California  Edison
KOA will coordinate  with  Southern  California  Edison  (SCE) for the proposed  electrical  design  required  for
the proposed  intersection  safety  lighting.  We will coordinate  our design  and service  loads with  the SCE
service  planner  to determine  service  points  and design.

City  of Huntington  Park
KOA will coordinate  with  the City of Huntington  Park for the review  and approval  of the California
Avenue/Santa  Ana Street  traffic  signal  plan. We will revise the  traffic signal plan per the City's comments
and coordinate  approval  as required.

Utility  Relocation  Coordination
We have reviewed  the proposed  improvements  and have determined  that  no major  utility  relocation
coordination  will be required.  Utility  adjustments  on this project  have been  determined  to be minor  in
nature  (adjust  to grade).  KOA will coordinate  with  the City of South  Gate Water  Department  for the
relocation  of fire hydrants.

Utility  Potholing
C Below  will perform  utility  potholing  for the project.  At the time  we are assuming  four  (4) potholes  will be
required  at the intersection  of California  Avenue/Sanata  Ana Street.  A standard  pothole is 12 in x 12 in,
10-foot  maximum  depth,  performed  to the top  of pipe or encasement.  Potholes  will be repaired  with  a
sand backfill  and a permanent  surface  patch.  We are assuming  that  full concrete  sidewalk  panel  repair  will
not be required.

TASK  3 - RECORDS  RESEARCH  AND  FIELD REVIEWS
Records  Research
KOA will work  with  the City to obtain  record  drawings  and documents  relevant  to the project  corridor.
Record  drawings  and documents  can include,  but are not limited  to existing  improvement  plans,
topographic  maps,  assessor  maps,  centerline  ties, corner  records,  as-built  plans,  utility  plans, traffic  counts,
previous  traffic  studies,  etc. We will send our requests  for record  drawings  and documents  through  the
City's  Project  Manager.

Field  Review  & Site Evaluation
Upon  receipt  of the topographic  survey  any available  as-built  records  from  the City, we will visit the
project  site to fully evaluate  existing  conditions.  We will:
  *  Verify  record  drawings.
  *  Investigate  and verify  existing  roadway  geometry,  including  striping,  pavement  markings,  and
  signage.
  Verify  existing  pull boxes,  utility  manholes/valves,  traffic  signal  poles/equipment,  street  lighting,
  power  poles,  cabinets,  fire hydrants,  etc.
  *  We will document  the site visit with  photos  and field  notes.

Base Plan  Preparation
Upon  completion  of our field  review,  we will prepare  accurate  base plans.  The base plan will show  existing
centerlines,  curb, gutter,  sidewalk,  landscaping,  right-of-way,  curb ramps,  driveways,  pavement
delineations,  markings,  roadside  signs,  pull boxes,  utility  manholes/valves, power  poles,  fire hydrants,  and

  maintece  services necessary for the newly installed landscape improvements  within tJhe
  Tweedy Mile District.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The City Council will consider:

  a. Approving Amendment No. 2 to Contract No, 2024-82-CC with Mariposa Landscape
  Services, LLC. ("Agreement'5),  to secure additional landscape maintenance services
  necessary for the newly installed landscape improvements  located witMn the Tweedy
  Mile District as well as to perform one-time landscape and irrigation improvements at six
  median locations along Firestone Boulevard,  in an amount not to exceed $205,690;  and

  b. Authorizing  the Mayor  to execute Amendment  No. 2 in a form acceptable to the City
  Attorney.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  Atnendnient  No. 2 is in the amount of $205,690 and will be funded with
  Street Lighting and Landscaping  Maintenance  District (SL&LMD)  Funds. Funding will be
  budgeted in Fiscal Years 2026/27 and 2027/28 through the Public Works Department operating
  budgets, as summarized below. The SL&LMD  Fund is in a deficit, thus related expenditures are
  typically  subsidized by the General Fund and restricted funds such as the Gas Tax and
  transportation funds,

  Seone  of Work  FY 2026/27  FY 2027/28  Amendment  No-  2
  Tweedy  Mile Maintenance  $91,380  $91,380  $182,760
  Firestone  Median  l'mprovements  $22,930  $22,930
  Total  $114,310  $91,380  $205,690

  ANALYSIS:  The City contracts with Mariposa to provide citywide landscaping and general
  maintenance services for landscaped medians, commercial  corridors, parking lots, and other
  City-owned  facilities. Recently, new landscaped areas were installed withiii the Tweedy Mile

  102
 District  as part  of corridor  beautification  improvements.  These  landscaped  areas now  require
ongoing  maintenance  to preserve  plant  health,  maintain  aesthetic  quality,  and ensure  the long-
term  sustainability  of the improvements.

Amendment  No.  2 will  expand  Mariposa's  existing  scope  of  work  to  include  maintenance
services  for  the newly  landscaped  areas within  the Tweedy  Mile  perimeter.  Services  include
hand watering  twice  per week,  maintenance  of flower  beds, replacement  of plant  materials,  and
annual  mulch  refreshment.  Mariposa  submitted  a proposal  dated May  12, 2026,  in the amount  of
$7,615  per  month,  or  $91,380 annually.  The  proposed  amendment  includes  two  years  of
maintenance  services  totaling  $182,760.

In  addition,  six  unfinished  landscape  median  cut-out  locations  along  Firestone  Boulevard
currently  remain  unimproved.  These  locations  consist  of exposed  dirt  areas within  landscaped
medians  that were  intended  for future  landscaping  improvements.  The proposed  work  includes
removal  of  unsuitable  material,  extension  of  drip  irrigation,  placement  and  compaction  of
decomposed  granite,  and installation  of forty-eight  (48)  five-gallon  Foxtail  Agaves.  Mariposa
submitted  a proposal  dated  May  20,  2026,  in  the  amount  of  $22,930  to  complete  the
improvements.

Approval  of Amendment  No.  2 will  ensure  that the Tweedy  Mile  landscape  improvements  are
properly  maintained  and that  the remaining  median  landscaping  along  Firestone  Boulevard  is
completed  consistent  with  the City's  beautification  objectives  and maintenance  standards.

BACKGROUND:  The City  operates  and maintains  landscaping  and irrigation  systems  located
throughout  public  streets,  landscape  medians,  parking  lots,  and  other  City-owned  facilities.
Under  Contract  No.  2024-82-CC,  Mariposa  Landscape  Services  provides  citywide  landscaping
and general  maintenance  services,  including  landscape  maintenance,  irrigation  system  repairs,
trash  abatement,  pressure  washing,  weed  control,  and  other  related  grounds  maintenance
activities.

On October  22, 2024,  the City  Council  approved  Contract  No. 2024-82-CC  with  Mariposa  in the
amount  of $1,361,016  for annual  citywide  landscaping  and general  maintenance  services  for  a
three-year  term.  On  July  8, 2025,  the  City  Council  approved  Amendment  No.  I to expand
services  associated  with  newly  constructed  medians  and restoration  projects  throughout  the City
for a not-to-to-exceed  amount  of $451,370.

Since  approval  of Amendment  No. 1, additional  landscaping  improvements  have been installed
within  the Tweedy  Mile  District  that were not included  in the original  Agreement  or Amendment
No.  1. These  newly  landscaped  areas now  require  ongoing  maintenance  services  to preserve
plant  health,  maintain  aesthetic  quality,  and  ensure  the  long-term  sustainability  of  the
improvements.  Amendment  No.  2 provides  $91,380  annually  to fund  landscape  maintenance
services  within  the Tweedy  Mile  District.

Additionally,  several  unfinished  landscape  cut-out  areas  remain  along  Firestone  Boulevard
medians.  These  locations  were  originally  intended  to receive  landscaping  improvements  but
currently  consist  of exposed  dirt areas within  the median  islands.  Amendment  No. 2 will  provide
irrigation  and landscaping  improvements  at six locations  to complete  the median  enhancements
and improve  corridor  aesthetics.

two term extensions. The extensions will be at the City Manager's discretion based on the
recommendations for the Department of Public Works and the successful performance of
Mariposa.

BACKGROUND:  The City owns facilities citywide that require landscaping and general
maintenance services, This includes facilities such as landscaped road medians, city-owned
vacant properties, retaining walls, bus shelters, sidewalks, parking lots, the Tweedy Mile District,
and the Hollydale Shopping Center, The Department of Public Works maintains these facilities
through the services of a maintenance contractor that provide annual maintenance services as
well as emergency responses services. Currently, these facilities are maintained by Parkwood,
under ContractNo, 2021-127-CC. The agreement expires on October 31, 2024.

On August 19, 2024, a Request for Proposal ("RFP") was issued to procure a new contract. On
September 12, 2024, two proposals were received in the City Clerk's Office, as sunnmarized on
the next page. A panel comprised of the Streets Supervisor and the Streets and Sewer

sector contracts, directly related public sector experience, and expertise levels.

municipal contracts, and resource availability. They possess the resources, eqipment  and

 BACKGROUND:  The  California  Department  of  Resources  Recycling  and  Recovery
(CalRecycle)  administers  the Used  Oil  Recycling  Grant  Program  and the Beverage  Container
Recycling  Grant  Program  to  support  local  recycling  and  environmental  protection  efforts
throughout  California.  These  programs  provide  funding  to local  governrnents  and other  eligible
organizations  to expand  recycling  opportunities,  reduce pollution,  and increase  public  participation
in recycling  programs.

The Used  Oil Recycling  Grant  Program  was established  through  the Used  Oil Recycling  Act  of
1991  (SB 546) and supports  activities  that encourage  the proper  collection  and recycling  of used
motor  oil.  The  program  helps  prevent  improper  disposal  of used  oil,  which  can contaminate
waterways,  soil, and other environmental  resources.

The Beverage  Container  Recycling  Grant  Program  was established  under  the Beverage  Container
Recycling  and Litter  Reduction  Act  of 1986,  which  created  California's  California  Redemption
Value  (CRV)  recycling  system.  The program  supports  recycling  infrastructure,  public  education,
and activities  that  increase  the recovery  and recycling  of eligible  beverage  containers  while
reducing  litter.

Through  these  grant  programs,  John  L.  Hunter  and  Associates,  Inc.  provides  program
administration  services  on behalf  of the City,  including:  (a) public  education  and outreach,  (b)
recycling  center  support  and administration,  (c) coordination  with  stormwater,  used oil recycling,
and beverage  container  recycling  programs;  and (d) general  grant administration.

Collectively,  these  grant-'Junded  activities  help  protect  the environment  by reducing  pollution,
preventing  hazardous  materials  from  entering  waterways  and  landfills,  reducing  litter,  and
promoting  recycling  within  the community.

  1985.  We specialize  in assisting municipalities  implement  water  quality  and conservation

2, Scope of Work  and Project  Understanding

We welcome  the opportunity  to continue  providing  as-needed  professional  Used Oil Recycling
and Beverage  Container  Grant  programs  services  to the City of South Gate. This section  details
the approach  tO COmplete  the SCOpe Of WOrk (SOW). The timeframe  Of thiS proposal  iS  far  a
period  of three  (3) years  (Fiscal Year 2023-2024  through  2025-2026)  with  the option  for a one
(1) year extension,  upon  written  agreement  by the City and JLHA. This proposal  is considered
valid for a period  of ninety  (90) days from the date of submittal.

2.1.  Used  Oil Recycling  and  Beverage  Container  Recycling  Grant  Programs

The Department  of Resources  Recycling  and Recovery  (CalRecycle)  distributes  an annual  grant to
the City specifically  for the Used Oil Recycling  and Beverage  Container  Recycling  programs.  JLHA
and the  City will  work  together  to implement  projects  to achieve  the goals  of the  Used Oil
Recycling  and Beverage  Container  Recycling  Grant program.  Below is an outline  of the tasks that
will  be implemented  during  each  reporting  year  for  both  Used  Oil Recycling  and  Beverage
Container  Recycling  programs.  These tasks aim to increase  the recycling  of used oil, filters,  and
beverage  containers,  and decrease  the volume  of oil and containers  discarded  into storm  drains
or public disposal  sites. All outreach  activities  and vendor  purchases  will have prior approval  from
the City.

BACKGROUND:  On November 6, 2018, the Safe, Clean Water Program ("Program"), known
as the Measure W ballot measure, was successfully passed by voters. The Program provides
local, dedicated funding to increase water supply, improve water quality, and provide cornrnunity
enhancements throughout Los Angeles County. The Program is a special parcel tax of 2.5 cents
per square foot of impermeable surface area for private property. Publicly owned parcels,
including schools, are exempt under state law. The Program was estimated to generate $285
million annually of which 10%, 40% and 50% is programmed for the Los Angeles County Flood
Control District, local agencies, and a Regional Program, respectively.

On September 15, 2021, the City was awarded a grant in the amount of $5,438,000 for
construction, water quality monitoring and operations and maintenance for the Urban Orchard
Project. The grant program required a resolution to enter into a Transfer Agreement with the Los
Angeles County Flood Control District to receive the funds.

On November 23, 2021, Resolution 2021-61-CC was approved by City Council to approve
Transfer Agreement No. 2021RPLLARO5  and authorize the Assistant City Manager/Director of
Public Works or designee as agent of the applicant to submit all documents pertaining to the
Transfer Agreement including, but not limited to, budget plans, payment requests, progress
reports, annual reports, and monitoring reports, operations and maintenance plans and other
documents, which may be necessary for the completion of the Urban Orchard Project.

Council to approve Addendum No. I to Transfer Agreement No. 2021RPLLARO5  and authorize
the Assistant City Manager/Director  of Public Works or designee as agent of the applicant to
submit all documents pertaining to the Transfer Agreement including, but not limited to, budget
plans, payment requests, progress reports, annual reports, and monitoring reports, operations and
maintenance plans and other documents, which may be necessary for the completion of the

Basic  Facts
Congress  created  the  NFIP  in 1968  in response  to the  rising  cost  of taxpayer-funded  disaster  relief  for flood  victims  and  the  increasing  amount  of
damage  caused  by floods.  The  NFIP  makes  federally  backed  flood  insurance  available  in communities  that  agree  to adopt  and  enforce  floodplain
management  ordinances  to reduce  future  flood  damage.  The  NFIP  is self-supporting  for the  average  historical  loss  year.  This  means  that  unless
there  is a widespread  disaster,  operating  expenses  and flood  insurance  claims  are financed  through  premiums  collected.

Commercial  buildings  or residential  dwellings  owned  by commercial  entities  are considered  commercial  property.  All others  are residential  dwellings
